slide_title: The Human Cardiovascular System: Structure of the Heart
original_text: The Human Cardiovascular System Structure of the Heart Septumseparates the heart into left & right sides Each side has two chambers Upper two chambers are the atria Thin-walled Receive blood from circulation Lower two chambers are the ventricles Thick-walled Pump blood away from heart
explanation: The human heart is divided internally into left and right halves by a muscular wall called the septum. This complete separation prevents oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing. The heart has four chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles. The atria are thin-walled because they only receive blood from systemic or pulmonary circulation and pump it a short distance into the ventricles. The ventricles are thick-walled because they must generate enough pressure to pump blood away from the heart to the lungs or the rest of the body.

questions.q: What is the function of the septum in the human heart?
opts: It regulates the rhythm of the heart as a pacemaker.
It separates the heart into left and right sides to prevent blood mixing.
It connects the atria directly to the aorta.
It acts as a valve to prevent backflow into the ventricles.
questions.exp: The septum is a muscular wall that completely separates the left and right sides of the heart, preventing oxygen-poor and oxygen-rich blood from mixing.

questions.q: Why are the walls of the ventricles thicker than the walls of the atria?
opts: The ventricles receive blood from the veins, which is under high pressure.
The ventricles must generate high pressure to pump blood out of the heart, whereas the atria only receive blood.
The ventricles contain pacemaker cells that require thick muscle fibers to generate electrical signals.
The ventricles are exposed to the external thoracic cavity.
questions.exp: Ventricles are thick-walled because they pump blood away from the heart into long vascular pathways under high pressure, while atria are thin-walled as they only receive blood.
